passages.t: One altar, and no other gods
passages.happening:
The LORD gives a command for “Aaron, his sons, and all the Israelites” (verse 2). Anyone who kills an ox, a lamb or a goat, in the camp or outside it, without bringing it to the entrance of the tent as an offering to the LORD, “shall incur bloodguilt. He has shed blood and must be cut off from among his people” (verse 4).

The sacrifices people have been making in the open fields are to be brought to the priest and offered ‘as sacrifices of peace to the LORD’ (verse 5).

“They must no longer offer their sacrifices to the goat demons to which they have prostituted themselves” (verse 7). The same holds for a foreigner living among them (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
A new part of the book begins here. Chapters 1 to 16 were mostly about the tent and how to come near to God. From chapter 17 to chapter 26 the book carries holiness out into the whole of life. Since 1877, when the German scholar August Klostermann gave it the name, this part has been called the Holiness Code.

It begins with blood, the subject that joins the two halves.

In Israel, as across the ancient world, meat was not everyday food. Most families ate it on a feast day or when a guest came, and killing an animal was often an act of worship as much as butchery. This law takes that custom and gives it one place. Every ox, lamb or goat killed is to be brought to the tent and made a peace offering: part to God, part to the priest, the rest a meal for the family, eaten before the LORD.

The reason is in verse 7. In that world the desert and the open country were widely thought to be the home of spirits that had to be kept content. An animal killed in a field could easily become a gift to them. The law shuts that door. Israel's worship is to go to one God at one altar.

The strong word ‘bloodguilt’ shows how seriously the life of an animal is taken. To kill one carelessly, away from God, is counted as shedding blood.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy, looking ahead to life in a wide land where the sanctuary would be days away, allows ordinary meat to be killed at home: “whenever you want, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your gates” (Deuteronomy 12:15). But it keeps the rule about blood: “you must not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water” (Deuteronomy 12:16).

Later history shows the danger verse 7 names. King Jeroboam “appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat demons and calf idols he had made” (2 Chronicles 11:15).

Paul says the same of the sacrifices of his own day: they are offered ‘to demons, not to God’ (1 Corinthians 10:20).
passages.hard:
This chapter says every animal must be killed at the tent. Deuteronomy 12 lets people kill meat at home. Do the laws contradict each other?

Readers explain the difference in several ways. Many traditional interpreters see Leviticus as a law for the wilderness camp, where everyone lived near the tent, and Deuteronomy as Moses adjusting it for a large land; Deuteronomy itself gives distance as its reason. Some Jewish interpreters read this chapter more narrowly, as being only about animals meant as sacrifices. Many critical scholars think the two laws come from different circles or times.

On any reading the two laws agree on two things. Blood belongs to God. And sacrifice must not drift away to other gods or other altars.
passages.asks: Israel was not to make small, private offerings to other powers on the side. Ask what you quietly trust to keep you safe besides God: money, luck, a person, a habit. And ask whether your ordinary meals and ordinary work are lived before God, or kept apart from him.

passages.t: The life is in the blood
passages.happening:
“If anyone from the house of Israel or a foreigner living among them eats any blood, I will set My face against that person and cut him off from among his people” (verse 10).

Then the reason: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar; for it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul” (verse 11).

A hunter who kills an animal or bird that may be eaten “must drain its blood and cover it with dirt” (verse 13). Anyone who eats an animal found dead or torn by beasts must wash, and is unclean until evening (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Verse 11 is among the most important sentences in Leviticus. For sixteen chapters blood has been put on the altar, sprinkled before the curtain and carried into the innermost room. Here, at last, God says why. He speaks in the first person.

Three things are packed into the verse.

Blood stands for life. When blood is poured out, a life is given up.

Atonement comes by a life given. The Hebrew of the last clause can be read in two ways: the blood atones by means of the life that is in it, or in exchange for a life, one life given for another. Both are good Hebrew.

And God gives it. ‘I have given it to you.’ In the ordinary way of thinking, a sacrifice is something people give to a god. This verse turns that round. The blood on the altar is God's gift to Israel before it is Israel's gift to God. It is his provision, never a bribe.

That is why blood must not be eaten. It is kept for one use. Life belongs to God, and its sign is not to be treated as ordinary food.

The rule is older than Israel, and wider. It was given to Noah, and here the foreigner living among Israel is named again and again.

Even a hunter's kill, which could not be brought to the altar, is treated with respect. Its blood is poured out and covered with earth. It is returned to the ground and not consumed.

Jewish practice built careful ways of killing and salting meat so that the blood is drained from it, and keeps them today.
passages.later:
God said to Noah, “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4).

The letter to the Hebrews rests on this verse: “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Hebrews 9:22). Paul writes of Christ, “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7).

Against this background the words of Jesus were shocking to those who first heard them: “unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you” (John 6:53). The law kept blood back because the life belonged to God. Jesus offers his own life to be received. Christians differ on how that is so in the Lord's Supper. They agree that his life, given, is the source of theirs.
passages.hard:
Why blood? And must Christians keep from eating it?

On the first question, the note on Hebrews 9:15-22 says more. In short: in Israel the sacrifice was God's own provision, given in mercy so that sinners could live. It was never a way of buying off an angry god.

On the second, Christians have answered in more than one way. The leaders in Jerusalem asked Gentile believers to keep from blood (Acts 15:29). Many read that as a request suited to its setting, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share one table, and hold that Christians are free in what they eat (Mark 7:19). Some Christians hold that the request still stands. The note on Acts 15:12-21 sets out the readings, and these notes take no side.

One caution. This verse is about eating blood and about sacrifice. It was not written about modern medicine, and these notes are not medical advice. A person facing a decision about medical treatment should talk with a doctor.
passages.asks: ‘I have given it to you.’ The means of coming back to God was his gift before it was anyone's offering. Ask whether you think of forgiveness as something you must get from God, or something he has already moved to give. And ask how you treat life, human and animal, in a world that spends it cheaply.
